Learning Objectives
Understand the pathophysiology of postoperative adverse local tissue reaction.
Review the potential sources of metal particulate wear.
Discuss the evaluation of patients with an adverse local tissue reaction.
Review common treatment options for patients with pseudotumor because of an adverse local
tissue reaction.

Lymphocyte-dominated adverse local tissue reaction (ALTR) may form secondary to the
generation of metal wear debris particles in total hip arthroplasty (THA).
ALTR often is attributed to metal-on-metal (MoM) articulating surfaces and non-articulating
metal prosthetic interfaces in THA.
Elevated serum ion levels are associated with abnormal functioning of a MoM articulation.
ALTR is associated with osteolysis, tissue necrosis, and pseudotumor formation (Figure 1).
Figure 1 Images show adverse location tissue reaction. A, Axial T1-weighted metal-artifact
reduction sequence MRI of a right hip shows a large, hyperintense, heterogeneous fluid collection
(white arrow) extending from the hip joint into the anteromedial thigh. B, Intraoperative
photograph of the hip shows profound metallosis with severe destruction of the periarticular
structures. C, Histopathologic image shows chronic inflammation in the pericapsular tissue, with
mild perivascular inflammatory infiltrate unique to an aseptic lymphocyte-dominant vasculitis-
associated lesion (hematoxylin-eosin stain, magnification ×40). (Reproduced from Bolognesi MP,
Ledford CK: Metal-on-metal total hip arthroplasty: Patient evaluation and treatment. J Am Acad
Orthop Surg 2015;23[12]:724-731.)

Overview
Aseptic lymphocyte-dominant vasculitis-associated lesions (ALVALs) are a potential result
of MoM THA articulations and modular prostheses with metallic interfaces. The disease
results from small particle wear that causes destruction of the tissues surrounding THA.
This reaction may result in a mass-like or fluid-filled lesion known as a pseudotumor.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Adverse Local Tissue Reaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000509
2/28

These lesions are neither infectious nor malignant, and they account for a considerable
proportion of revisions of MoM THA implants.
Epidemiology
Pseudotumors occur in 10% to 15% of patients with a MoM THA implant; however, some cases
are clinically silent.
Approximately 50% of MoM THA revision procedures are performed secondary to
pseudotumor formation.
The failure rate of MoM articulations is estimated to be two to three times that of non-MoM
bearings.

Epidemiology
MoM implants were first introduced in 1966 with the McKee-Farrar prosthesis.1 Since
1996, more than 1 million hip prostheses with MoM articulations have been implanted.
Their theoretic advantages over conventional metal-on-polyethylene implants, including
larger-diameter heads, resulting in fewer dislocations2 and lower implant wear rates,3
which make them attractive as bearing options; however, registry data have since
demonstrated a twofold to threefold increase in revision rates compared with other
modern hip implants.4 Risk factors that predispose MoM implants to failure include
elevated cobalt-chromium levels, female sex, femoral head sizes 36 mm or larger,
monoblock acetabular components, functional acetabular designs that do not represent
a full hemisphere, and acetabular inclination angles greater than 50° (Figure 2; Resource
1).

Figure 2 AP radiograph of a pelvis demonstrates bilateral metal-on-metal total hip
arthroplasty. The right acetabular component is excessively abducted compared with the
well-positioned left acetabular component. (Reproduced from Bolognesi MP, Ledford CK:
Metal-on-metal total hip arthroplasty: Patient evaluation and treatment. J Am Acad
Orthop Surg 2015;23[12]:724-731.)
Biomechanics
Low linear wear rates of MoM THA bearings allow for thinner acetabular components and
larger femoral heads compared with metal-on-polyethylene bearings, resulting in the
following:
Increased jump distance to dislocation
Greater range of motion arc and resultant increase in range of motion to impingement
Less volumetric wear than metal-on-polyethylene bearings
Bearing surface relies on elastohydrodynamic film to support the applied load SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Adverse Local Tissue Reaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000509
4/28

Sensitive to cup positioning and femoral head clearance

Biomechanics
The wear characteristics of MoM prostheses generally are characterized by a “run-in”
wear rate, which usually occurs in the first 1 million cycles, followed by a “steady-state
wear rate with decreased particle generation. Current-generation MoM bearings (high-
carbon, wrought cobalt-chromium alloy) with a 28-mm femoral head diameter are
associated with a mean in vivo wear rate of 27.8 μm per year for the first year of use and
6.2 μm per year after the second year, with femoral heads generally exhibiting a higher
wear rate than acetabular cups. Serum metal ion concentrations are highest 1 to 2 years
after the index procedure.5
Clearance, the difference between the diameter of the femoral head and the diameter of
the acetabular cup, is a factor that influences wear in MoM bearings. Clearances of 100
to 200 μm maximize the fluid film thickness by entrapping joint fluid between the two
bearing surfaces. Clearances that are too high result in increased wear, whereas
clearances that are too low may result in clamping; complete loss of space and direct
MoM wear; and/or equatorial seizing, which involves high frictional torques between the
femoral head and the acetabular rim because of deformation of the cup during
impaction. A larger femoral head diameter increases the entrainment velocity, the speed
with which the fluid is brought into the joint, maximizing fluid film lubrication. Mixed film
lubrication, in which abrasive wear results from direct contact of the bearing surfaces,
likely occurs most frequently in vivo, even with an ideal head diameter and clearance5
(Figure 3).

Figure 3 Image of a total hip arthroplasty implant. Clearance is defined as the difference
in the radius of the inner diameter of the acetabular cup and the radius of the outer
diameter of the femoral head. A deforming force applied to the acetabular component at
the time of insertion reduces the radius of the inner surface of the acetabular shell,
which reduces overall clearance. (Reproduced with permission from Springer BD, Habet
NA, Griffin WL, Nanson CJ, Davies MA: Deformation of 1-piece metal acetabular
components. J Arthroplasty 2012;27[1]:48-54.)
The overall volume of wear of MoM prosthetic joint surfaces has been related to the
presence of a minimum elastohydrodynamic fluid film thickness for the mean surgical
conditions of load, speed, viscosity, and elasticity of the metals used in each prosthesis.
This is referred to as the lambda ratio, or the ratio of the thickness of the fluid film to the
composite root mean square surface roughness. A lambda ratio of 1 or less in a MoM
bearing results in severe mixed lubrication conditions. A lambda ratio of 3 or greater
indicates that fluid film lubrication is adequate to substantially reduce the effect of load
and, therefore, minimize friction and wear. Lower clearance and larger femoral head
sizes promote higher lambda ratios, as demonstrated by the calculation below.6

thickness and the component’s arithmetic mean roughness (Ra):

Contact patch–to-rim (CPR) distance is the distance between the point of application of
the joint reaction force and the rim of the acetabular implant in a patient in the standing
position. An inverse relationship exists between wear and CPR distance. The mean CPR
distance is approximately 14 mm. A CPR distance of less than 5 mm is associated with
increased metal ion levels and increased rates of prosthetic loosening, wear, and
dislocation. Factors that result in decreased CPR distance include a high abduction angle,
excessive anteversion of the acetabular implant, and cup designs with smaller arcs of
coverage of the femoral head (ie, non-hemispheric cups; (Figure 4).

Figure 4 Illustrations of total hip arthroplasty implants show the contact patch–to-rim
distance. Left, Edge loading does not occur because the contact patch is within the inner
surface of the acetabular cup. Right, Edge loading occurs because the contact patch
extends over the rim of the acetabular cup. (Reproduced with permission from Hua X, Li
J, Jin Z, Fisher J: The contact mechanics and occurrence of edge loading in modular metal-
on-polyethylene total hip replacement during daily activities. Med Eng Phys
2016;38[6]:518-525.)
Etiology
MoM THA bearings generate nanometer-sized particles that can dissolve to generate cobalt
(Co2+) and low-valence chromium (Cr3+) ions.
Two types of immunologic responses are theorized:
Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity response
Local response to high levels of wear debris
Immune response to metal particles may result in osteolysis.
The presence of metal particles may lead to a pathologic soft tissue finding known as an
ALVAL, or a pseudotumor.
Fluid collection or a solid mass may be observed in the periprosthetic soft tissues.
May result in destruction of the abductor muscle group
Pseudotumor has been reported in painful and well-functioning prostheses; however, the
degree of implant wear has not yet been directly correlated with the severity of ALTRs (Figure
5).

Figure 5 Hematoxylin-eosin histologic images obtained at magnifications of ×5 (A) and ×20 (B)
show the diffuse perivascular infiltrates of T and B lymphocytes along with plasma cells and
macrophages with or without metal debris. These findings are characteristic of aseptic
lymphocyte-dominant vasculitis-associated lesions. (Reproduced from Taunton MJ, Amanatullah
DF: Taper corrosion after total hip arthroplasty: Evaluation and management, in Lieberman, JR,
Berry DJ, eds: Advanced Reconstruction: Hip, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 437-447.)

Etiology
MoM THA–generated wear debris particles are approximately 10 to 50 nm in size. These
particles can dissolve and form cobalt (Co2+) and chromium (Cr3+) ions, which are
detectable in blood and urine because of their renal excretion. The British Medicines and
Healthcare products Regulatory Agency has suggested a cutoff level of 7 parts per billion
for cobalt and chromium levels; however, the 7 parts per billion cutoff level is associated
with a specificity of 89% and a sensitivity of 52% in detecting failed MoM THA implants7
and should not be solely relied on as a screening test. With high wear levels, local soft
tissues are subject to potential metaplasia; however, little evidence has suggested an
overall increased risk of malignancy. Systemic cytotoxicity of elevated metal ion levels is
not fully understood; therefore, MoM articulations are relatively contraindicated in
females of childbearing age because elevated metal ion levels have been detected in the
placental blood of mothers with MoM THAs.8 Patients with renal insufficiency may be at
increased risk for systemic adverse effects because of their decreased ability to clear
metal ions.9
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Adverse Local Tissue Reaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000509
9/28

Two types of local soft-tissue reactions have been proposed, with the lymphocyte being
the predominant cell type in both (Resource 2). One such reaction is a type IV (delayed)
hypersensitivity response characterized by a perivascular infiltrate of T lymphocytes
because of the presence of metalloprotein complexes. Metal particles under
phagocytosis by macrophages, which act as antigen-presenting cells to T lymphocytes,
result in cell-mediated type IV hypersensitivity reaction10 (Resource 3). The presence of
plasma cells, B lymphocytes, and massive fibrin exudation not characteristic of a type IV
(delayed) hypersensitivity reaction have been described as an ALVAL.11 The ultimate
macroscopic response may include osteolytic, necrotic cystic, and mass-forming lesions.
Modular Implants
All metal modular junctions have the potential to release metal ions because of corrosion,
wear, and micromotion, with each additional interface in a prosthesis increasing the number
of potential areas of failure12 (Resource 4).
Modularity typically occurs at a Morse taper. The male portion of the taper (trunnion)
compresses the female portion (eg, the bore in the femoral head), interlocking the two
components in axial and rotational directions.
Modularity may facilitate the exchange of components during revision arthroplasty.
Head-neck modularity of a femoral THA implant allows intraoperative flexibility to address leg
length and offset and, to a lesser degree, the head-neck ratio.
Dual modular neck designs involve a double taper, in which the Morse taper, or trunnion of
the distal part of the neck, engages with the proximal stem, allowing for additional versatility
and the ability to adjust length, offset, and neck version.
In 2012, a voluntary product recall of a modular femoral neck stem was announced because
of a high revision rate secondary to metal debris from the metal junctions (trunnions).

Modular Implants
Implant modularity between the head-neck and neck-stem junctions affords increased
flexibility in adjusting the proximal portion of the femoral implant. Head-neck modularity
also allows for modification in two dimensions to address leg length and offset, and

neck-stem modularity allows for modification of femoral neck version and leg length and
offset; however, each metallic interface/junction present in the prosthesis is susceptible
to the effects of corrosion12 (Figures 6 and 7).
Figure 6 Intraoperative (A) and clinical (B) photographs of a total hip arthroplasty
implant with a dual modular neck show deposition of chromium(III) phosphate because
of fretting and crevice corrosion at the femoral head-neck junction (A) and the stem-neck
junction (B). (Reproduced from Taunton MJ, Amanatullah DF: Taper corrosion after total
hip arthroplasty: Evaluation and management, in Lieberman, JR, Berry DJ, eds: Advanced
Reconstruction: Hip, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2017, pp 437-447.)

Figure 7 AP radiographs of the hip of a patient with a dual modular femoral neck stem
demonstrate trochanteric osteolysis (white arrow) adjacent to the neck-stem modular
junction (black arrow). (Reproduced with permission from Kwon YM: Evaluation of the
painful dual taper modular neck stem total hip arthroplasty: Do they all require revision?
J Arthroplasty 2016;31[7]:1385-1389.)
Several types of corrosion can occur at a metal prosthetic interface. Fretting corrosion
results from micromotion between two surfaces, which may disrupt the protective oxide
layer formed by self-passivation in titanium implants. Reports suggest that less fretting
may occur if a ceramic head is mated with a cobalt-chromium trunnion. Galvanic
corrosion results from electrochemical transfer of charges between two dissimilar
metals in the presence of fluid (ie, a cobalt-chromium femoral head on a titanium alloy
stem). Crevice corrosion occurs if crevices at the Morse taper allow fluid to enter, which
creates local conditions that encourage oxidation. The incidence of crevice corrosion in
retrieval studies is as high as 35% to 40% with mixed-metal tapers and 9% to 28% with
single-alloy components. This is thought to be the dominant type of corrosion in
trunnionosis.1

Risk factors associated with trunnion corrosion include the use of large cobalt-chromium
femoral heads that may generate increased torsional forces. Tapers with decreased
rigidity, such as narrow cone-angled tapers and those with shorter taper lengths that
allow for less interference fit, have increased micromotion between components.
Dissimilar alloy pairings may increase the risk of galvanic corrosion. Intraoperative
surgical assembly also may play an important role because in vitro studies have
demonstrated greatly reduced load to failure (>50%) at the stem-neck interface with a
contaminated assembly compared with a well-cleaned assembly. Patient factors that
may contribute to increased levels of corrosion include higher body mass index, longer
implantation time, and higher activity levels.12
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Obtain pertinent information regarding the index procedure.1
Date, location, surgeon
Indication
Adverse events or complications during perioperative course (ie, delayed wound healing)
History of metal hypersensitivity
Surgical report and implants used
Onset, frequency, and severity of pain1
MoM implants have been associated with a higher incidence of groin pain compared with
alternative articulations.
Diagnosis of head-neck junction corrosion may be difficult.
Clinical presentation may vary and includes no symptoms, pain, palpable masses, limp
secondary to abductor damage, late recurrent instability, and catastrophic implant failures.

Patient History
Pain after THA with a MoM articulation or modular components may be intrinsic or
extrinsic in nature13 (Resource 5). Examples of pain intrinsic to arthroplasty include
acute or chronic infection, aseptic loosening, instability, fracture, impingement, and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Adverse Local Tissue Reaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000509
13/28

ALVALs. Similar to any patient with a painful THA, infection should always be high on the
list of differential diagnoses. The patient should be questioned about recent illnesses,
infections, and history of wound drainage. Intra-articular pathology most commonly
manifests as deep-seated groin pain. MoM implants have been associated with a higher
incidence of groin pain than other articulations. Patient perceptions of soft-tissue
masses or fluid collections may be an indicator of ALTR to metal wear particles. Insidious
development of a limp and recurrent instability may be signs of abductor damage
secondary to metallosis. Rare systemic implications of cobalt toxicity, ranging from
neuro-ocular damage to hypothyroidism to cardiomyopathy, have been reported.14
Physical Examination
Scar location may indicate the approach used for the index procedure.
Careful neurovascular examination
Examination for signs of infection
Large pseudotumors may manifest as palpable fluid collections or soft-tissue masses.
Abduction weakness or Trendelenburg gait may result from abductor destruction.

Physical Examination
On physical examination, range of motion of the hip should be assessed, and any pain,
catching, or grinding should be noted. The wound should be assessed for drainage, sinus
tracts, and other signs of periprosthetic infection. Palpable fluid collection or masses
may indicate a pseudotumor. Although neurologic deficits are rare, femoral and sciatic
nerve palsies secondary to pseudotumor lesions have been reported; therefore, a
careful neurologic examination should be performed. Careful assessment of abductor
strength is paramount because the muscle group may be compromised by an ALTR
given its proximity to the bearing surface and the modular taper junction.13
Imaging Studies

Radiographic evaluation may reveal cystic lesions or areas of osteolysis near the femoral and
acetabular components.
Metal-artifact reduction sequence (MARS) MRI is sensitive and specific for the detection of
pseudotumor. CT with metal artifact reduction may be beneficial in evaluating the extent of
osteolysis, if present, and may provide information on component fixation.
Ultrasonography is a cost-effective method of evaluating the soft tissues adjacent to the
implant but may be user dependent.
May be used to guide aspiration or biopsy
Radiography
AP pelvis, AP hip, cross-table lateral hip
Evaluate for
Implant positioning
Implant design
Osteolysis or loosening (Figures 8 and 9; Resource 6)

Radiography
Careful review of initial and postoperative radiographs may reveal important
information, such as implant type, size, and positioning.1 Larger femoral head sizes in
MoM articulations have been associated with higher revision rates in registry studies.4

9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Adverse Local Tissue Reaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000509
16/28

Similarly, the presence of certain implant designs, such as dual modular necks, may
increase suspicion for metal wear–induced pathology. Increased cup abduction angles of
50° or more have been associated with higher levels of serum and synovial metal ions.13
Osteolysis because of metal wear debris may manifest as cystic lesions or radiolucent
regions near the femoral and acetabular components on plain radiographs. Erosion of
the calcar may be an early sign of osteolysis because of metal debris wear.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MARS MRI is useful in evaluating for pseudotumor (Figure 10).
Can be used to diagnose and monitor soft-tissue damage in patients at risk for revision
arthroplasty
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Adverse Local Tissue Reaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000509
17/28

Figure 10 Coronal metal-artifact reduction sequence MRI of a pelvis shows pseudotumors
surrounding bilateral metal-on-metal hip resurfacings. (Reproduced from Perry KI, MacDonald SJ:
The evaluation of metal-on-metal total hip arthroplasty, in Lieberman, JR, Berry DJ, eds: Advanced
Reconstruction: Hip, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp
423-429.)

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MARS MRI can improve visualization of the soft tissues by reducing 90% of the artifact
produced by the implant. Early signs of ALVALs include joint effusion, capsular
thickening, and synovitis. Edema also may be present in the pericapsular musculature. In
advanced disease, complex cystic or solid masses may be present. MARS MRI is
associated with a high sensitivity and specificity for the detection of pseudotumor and
can detect the presence of lesions in otherwise asymptomatic patients with MoM
articulations. Characteristic findings of MARS MRI that suggest revision surgery may be
beneficial include a progressive increase in the size of the pseudotumor, muscle
involvement, and substantial bony destruction.13
Diagnosis
Infection always must be considered and ruled out by obtaining appropriate inflammatory
markers.
Serum metal ion levels (cobalt and chromium) should be obtained in all symptomatic patients
with a MoM articulation or those with radiographic changes.
A low threshold for aspiration should exist because this allows clinicians to discern ALVALs
from periprosthetic joint infection.
Manual cell count should be performed to avoid a false-positive interpretation because of
cellular and metal debris.
Cross-sectional imaging modalities, such as ultrasonography or MARS MRI, are essential in the
work up and diagnosis of pseudotumor.

Diagnosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Adverse Local Tissue Reaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000509
18/28

Similar to the evaluation of any painful arthroplasty implant, infection must be near the
top of the differential diagnosis. Serum erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive
protein levels should be obtained as part of the laboratory evaluation. Serum metal ion
levels also should be obtained in patients with a poorly functioning MoM articulation and
patients with evidence of radiographic change. A cutoff value of 7 parts per billion or 7
μg/L generally has been accepted as an indication for advanced imaging studies in
patients with a MoM articulation and is associated with a sensitivity of 52% and a
specificity of 89% in testing for failed MoM THA.7 In patients with metallosis stemming
from modular junctions, cobalt levels may be fourfold to fivefold higher than chromium
levels, and cobalt-to-chromium ion ratios of 2:1 or higher should indicate advanced
imaging studies. A low threshold for hip aspiration should exist because this may help
differentiate ALVALs from periprosthetic infection. If hip aspiration is performed, a
manual cell count should be done because fibrinous debris from inflammatory metal
reactions may falsely elevate automated cell counts. MARS MRI is recommended for
symptomatic patients and those with elevated serum metal ion levels, regardless of
symptoms. If MRI is contraindicated, ultrasonography may be a reasonable alternative
imaging modality for the evaluation of soft tissues.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Asymptomatic patients with a well-functioning MoM articulation, few risk factors for ALVALs,
and low serum metal ion levels should be screened yearly.
Patients with risk factors for failure, such as poor implant positioning, radiographic changes,
poor implant track record, or elevated metal ion levels, may warrant closer follow-up.
Serum metal ion concentrations may help guide treatment of asymptomatic patients.

Nonsurgical Management
Patients with an existing, pain-free MoM THA implant may undergo observation. In
general, yearly radiographic follow-up is favored in patients with no obvious risk factors
for implant failure. Serum metal ion levels are a useful tool to evaluate MoM prosthetic
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Adverse Local Tissue Reaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000509
19/28

function and guide treatment of asymptomatic patients because as many as 60% of
ALVALs are clinically silent.15 Patients with elevated or up-trending metal ion levels may
warrant additional evaluation via advanced imaging studies; however, no clear
consensus currently exists on the timing for obtaining serum metal ion levels or
advanced imaging studies.
Surgical Management
A complete synovectomy and débridement of necrotic tissue at the time of surgical
management is necessary to remove nonviable tissue and reduce additional corrosion
(Figures 11 and 12; Resource 7).
Any loose or malpositioned implants should be revised.
MoM articulations should be replaced with metal-on-polyethylene or ceramic-on-polyethylene
articulations, depending on trunnion composition.
Modular tapered junctions with extensive corrosion warrant removal.
Strong consideration should be given to revising recalled femoral components or dual
modular tapered stems.

Surgical Management
At the time of surgery, the affected soft tissues should be débrided to prevent additional
progression of the ALVALs. Depending on the extent of the lesion, dissection around
neurovascular structures may be warranted and should be performed with care. Tissue
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Adverse Local Tissue Reaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000509
21/28

necrosis should prompt suspicion of low-grade infection. Intraoperative frozen section
and tissue cultures should be considered at the time of surgical management if infection
is suspected. Anterior, anterolateral, posterior, and direct lateral approaches for revision
of MoM components have been described in the literature. The posterolateral approach
is favored by some surgeons because of its extensile nature and versatility for femoral
and acetabular exposure.5,16,17 Success with revision of MoM components also has
been reported via anterior, anterolateral, and direct lateral approaches.18,19 Location
and accessibility of the pseudotumor and the exposure necessary to accomplish goals
should be considered in selecting a surgical approach. For example, femoral pathology
necessitating osteotomy for removal of well-fixed implants may be feasible but
technically demanding if addressed via a direct anterior approach. Although previous
incisions and surgical approaches should be used if possible, the ability to safely and
adequately address the current pathology be the first and foremost consideration.
Loose or malpositioned femoral or acetabular implants should be revised. MoM
articulations should be converted to ceramic-on-polyethylene or metal-on-polyethylene,
which necessitates removal of the acetabular cup in patients with a monoblock MoM
design. Modular acetabular components may be addressed by exchanging the metal
liner with a polyethylene liner in patients with a well-fixed cup that has the option of
switching liners. Limited data are available to support retention of a monoblock
acetabular component in combination with placement of a dual-mobility polyethylene
component. Concerns exist regarding increased polyethene wear against the metal
edges of the acetabular component. In addition, the use of dual-mobility constructs in
such single-component exchanges most commonly involve the use of a 22.2- or 28-mm
inner head, which only may be available in cobalt-chromium options depending on the
manufacturer. Such use of metal heads on trunnions with dissimilar metal composition
may potentiate corrosion and trunnionosis, introducing a secondary source of metal
debris. Highly porous metal implants may be used during reconstruction to maximize
bone ingrowth and decrease early aseptic loosening of the revision shell.13
Strong consideration should be given to removal of recalled femoral implants and those
with dual modular designs with evidence of taper corrosion. Well-fixed, nonmodular
femoral implants with head-neck junction taper corrosion may be addressed via femoral
head exchange. Stems with gross metal loss or fracturing of the trunnion require

revision. The composition of the new head often is determined by the composition of the
retained stem. At the time of revision, titanium alloy stems often are coupled with a
ceramic head with a titanium alloy sleeve. Cobalt-chromium alloy stems may be revised
to a sleeved ceramic head or a cobalt-chromium head, with no current consensus on
which option is optimal. Revision to a ceramic head without a titanium sleeve is not
recommended because of the risk of ceramic head fracture.
Careful assessment of stability is crucial to the success of revision surgery for ALVALs.
Postoperative instability is a concern because of the extensive resection of nonviable
capsule, soft tissue, and bone. Large femoral heads and dual-mobility designs can be
used as tools to increase the stability of the articulation. Abductor damage and
deficiency as a result of a pseudotumor must be addressed because of the high risk of
dislocation with potential loss of the abductor mechanism. Soft-tissue reconstruction or
the use of constrained liners should be considered if necessary (Figure 13).

Revision THA performed for ALVALs is associated with an increased risk for instability and
dislocation secondary to metallosis-induced damage to soft tissues, the need for extensive

Aseptic loosening, usually observed in the acetabular component, may occur in patients with
destructive ALVALs and pathologic acetabular bone.
Increased risks of infection have been reported with revision THA for metallosis.
Recurrence of pseudotumor is possible, most likely because of failure to remove all metal
debris or a secondary metal debris generator.

Complications
The most common reasons for re-revision after surgical management of ALVALs are
instability, aseptic loosening, and infection. Early complications are common, with re-
revision rates as high as 16% at 14-month follow-up.20 Instability is a major concern after
revision surgery because of metal particulate–induced necrosis of soft tissues and the
need for extensive débridement of metal debris at the time of surgery. Compromise of
the abductor complex and short external rotators may necessitate use of alternative
bearing designs, such as dual-mobility or constrained liners, to achieve long-term hip
stability.13
Revision arthroplasty for MoM implants has been shown to be associated with an
increased risk of postoperative infection. Some studies advocate extension of
postoperative oral antibiotic agents until finalization of intraoperative cultures.21 Positive
postoperative cultures after revision for the management of ALVALs warrant
consultation with an infectious disease specialist, and the species of bacteria and its
antibiotic susceptibilities should be determined. Often, a 6-week course of an
appropriate intravenous antibiotic agent is recommended, possibly followed by oral
suppression antibiotic treatment in patients who are not candidates for re-revision
surgery. In patients with recurrent prosthetic joint infection after antibiotic treatment, re-
revision surgery with explantation of components is warranted. The decision to manage
infection via a single- versus two-staged approach is an evolving topic and should be
made based on variables such as organism, bone stock, and health of the host.13
Bony destruction because of ALVALs also increases the risk of aseptic loosening of
revision components. This most commonly occurs at the acetabular implant, at which

of well-fixed acetabular components. This may increase the risk for failure of the revised
acetabular cup that still necessitates osseointegration. Recurrent or continued ALVALs
are a known entity and also may play a role in such complications. Failure to remove all
metal debris or recognize a secondary source of debris generation increases the risk of
continued ALTR. Therefore, revision of recalled implant designs, implants with poor track
records, and implants with dual modular tapered necks should be carefully considered.
Reduction in femoral component modularity, cleaning of the femoral trunnion before
placement of the femoral head, and forceful on-axis impaction of the femoral head at
the time of revision surgery have been advocated to decrease the risk of future taper
corrosion.
